doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Hamilton costs, fraternities and election night 1948
summary: He recalls tuition, the fraternity divide, being a leftist at a conservative school, and the chapel bell rung after Truman's win.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Well as long as we’re in this sort of part of your life, do you remember what it cost to go to Hamilton at the time?

I think it was three hundred bucks a semester. And then you had your room and board and that depended, because it was a bad situation at Hamilton at that time. You had sixty percent of the students who were in fraternities and forty percent were not. Now if you go to a place like Harvard where they had the Persallion and the fancy clubs, only a small fracture of the student body belonged to the clubs so you could ignore them. And if you went to places where they had a universal rushing policy, where everybody had to join if they wanted, then that was also a question. But at Hamilton you had the haves and the have nots so to speak. And it was always, there was always a problem about that. And I was — coming from a left wing family, see I didn’t belong at Hamilton. I wasn’t the right guy for Hamilton at all. It was a conservative school. There’s a wonderful story, in 1948 Truman of course won in that famous election where they all thought Dewey was going to win, but in fact there were only, in my fraternity, which was ELS, there were only two of us who were Democrats. One of them was a southern kid named Mort Sams, who was president of the house and I was Board Steward. And so we put out for the others, we put out cookies and coffee, and I had that all there and said “Well you guys are going to have a good time tonight.” But I sat up. And after around midnight I began thinking uh oh, something going on here. And finally by two or three in the morning it was becoming © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

clear that not only was Truman likely to win but we were going to have a Democratic congress. And I don’t think it was really until six or seven in the morning that it was finally decided. And so at nine o’clock in the morning some rascal went over and rang the chapel bell, as if it had been a football victory. And the dean, Dean Tolles, came flying out of his office shouting, “God damn it, I don’t care who won the election but God damn it this is a Republican college.”

I think it was Dean Tolles. It was one of them, either him or somebody else in the administration. But I was an old leftie, I had all this sort of Freudian thing in my background, and I had a lot — there were a lot of pre-ministerial students, I was an atheist, and these guys would just look at me as if I were a very strange creature. And they’d say, “Jim, you’re a nice guy, how can you be an atheist?” You know, that sort of thing.
